records.clean_question: A calculator is defective with probability $0.10$. If 10 calculators are selected independently, find the probability that at least 3 are defective.
records.clean_answer: Let $X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(10,0.1)$. Then $P(X\ge3)=1-P(X\le2)\approx1-0.9298=0.0702$.

records.clean_question: A calculator is defective with probability $0.10$. For 100 independently selected calculators, find the mean and standard deviation of the number of defectives.
records.clean_answer: For $X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(100,0.1)$, $\mu=np=10$ and $\sigma=\sqrt{np(1-p)}=\sqrt9=3$.

records.clean_question: Patient arrivals follow a Poisson process averaging 3 patients every 2 hours. Find the probability of exactly 6 arrivals during a 5-hour period.
records.clean_answer: The 5-hour mean is $\lambda=3(5/2)=7.5$. Thus $P(X=6)=e^{-7.5}7.5^6/6!\approx0.1367$.

records.clean_question: Patient arrivals follow a Poisson process averaging 3 patients every 2 hours. Find the probability of at least 4 but no more than 8 arrivals during a 3-hour period.
records.clean_answer: The 3-hour mean is $\lambda=4.5$. Therefore $P(4\le X\le8)=\sum_{x=4}^{8}e^{-4.5}4.5^x/x!\approx0.6174$.

records.clean_question: An auditor claims that exactly 10% of invoices contain errors. In a random sample of 20 invoices, 5 contain errors. Using $X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(20,0.10)$, assess the claim with the one-sided probability $P(X\ge5)$.
records.clean_answer: Under the claim, $P(X\ge5)=1-P(X\le4)\approx0.0432$. Because this probability is below 0.05, observing 5 or more errors is unusually unlikely under the claim; reject the claim at the 5% level. This is evidence against the claim, not proof that the true rate is different.

records.clean_question: An insurer charges a USD 1,500 annual premium for a USD 75,000 Hummer. The probability of theft is 0.0075. Find the insurer's expected net profit per policy.
records.clean_answer: Expected claim cost is $0.0075(75{,}000)=562.50$ dollars. Expected net profit is $1{,}500-562.50=937.50$ dollars.

records.clean_question: The probability of theft of a USD 75,000 Hummer is 0.0075. What premium should an insurer charge to obtain an expected net profit of USD 2,000 per policy?
records.clean_answer: If the premium is $c$, then $c-0.0075(75{,}000)=2{,}000$. Hence $c=2{,}562.50$ dollars.

A drug's six-month profit contribution is USD -30,000 with probability 0.2, USD 50,000 with probability 0.5, and USD 200,000 with probability 0.3. Management will market the drug only if expected profit exceeds USD 90,000. Decide.
records.clean_answer: $$E(X)=(-30{,}000)(0.2)+(50{,}000)(0.5)+(200{,}000)(0.3)=79{,}000\ \text{dollars}.$$ Since $79{,}000<90{,}000$, management should not market the drug under this rule.

records.clean_question: A lawyer has probability 0.3 of winning a case and earns USD 40,000 if she wins and nothing if she loses. She must spend USD 5,000 preparing the case in either outcome. Find her expected net gain.
records.clean_answer: The net gain is $35{,}000$ if she wins and $-5{,}000$ if she loses. Thus $E(X)=0.3(35{,}000)+0.7(-5{,}000)=7{,}000$ dollars.

records.clean_question: A vaccine is 95% effective. For 20 independent individuals, find the probability that it is ineffective for exactly one individual.
records.clean_answer: Let $X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(20,0.05)$. Then $P(X=1)=\binom{20}{1}(0.05)(0.95)^{19}\approx0.3774$.

records.clean_question: A vaccine is 95% effective. For 20 independent individuals, find the probability that it is ineffective for more than one individual.
records.clean_answer: With $X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(20,0.05)$, $P(X>1)=1-P(X=0)-P(X=1)\approx1-0.3585-0.3774=0.2641$.

records.clean_question: The probability that a reported residential-service problem is repaired the same day is 0.75. For the first five reported problems, find the mean and standard deviation of the number repaired the same day.
records.clean_answer: For $X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(5,0.75)$, $\mu=np=3.75$ and $\sigma=\sqrt{5(0.75)(0.25)}\approx0.9682$.

records.clean_question: Thirty percent of a cleaning company's jobs finish within the bid time. For a random sample of 8 jobs, find the probability that the number finished on time is within one standard deviation of its mean.
records.clean_answer: For $X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(8,0.3)$, $\mu=2.4$ and $\sigma=\sqrt{8(0.3)(0.7)}\approx1.296$. The integer values in [2.4-1.296, 2.4+1.296] dollars are 2 and 3, so $P(2\le X\le3)=P(X=2)+P(X=3)\approx0.2965+0.2541=0.5506$.

records.clean_question: A grocery-store service desk serves an average of 4 customers per half-hour. Assuming a Poisson distribution, find the probability that at most 2 customers use the desk in a half-hour.
records.clean_answer: For $X\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(4)$, $P(X\le2)=\sum_{x=0}^{2}e^{-4}4^x/x!\approx0.2381$.

records.clean_question: A grocery-store service desk serves an average of 4 customers per half-hour. Assuming a Poisson process, find the probability that exactly 2 customers use the desk in a one-hour period.
records.clean_answer: The one-hour mean is $\lambda=8$. Thus $P(X=2)=e^{-8}8^2/2!\approx0.0107$.

records.clean_question: State blood-program data claim that 40% of individuals have group A blood. In a random sample of 6, exactly 3 have group A blood. Using the one-sided probability $P(X\ge3)$ under $X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(6,0.4)$, assess the claim.
records.clean_answer: $P(X\ge3)=\sum_{x=3}^{6}\binom6x(0.4)^x(0.6)^{6-x}\approx0.4557$. This is not small, so 3 or more observations is not unusual under the claim; the sample does not provide evidence against the 40% rate.

records.clean_answer:

records.clean_question:
A bank's population waiting-time standard deviation is known to be $2.47$ minutes. For a random sample of 100 customers, $\bar x=5.46$. Investigate $H_0:\mu=6$ against $H_a:\mu<6$.

a. Describe the sampling distribution of $\bar X$.

b. Find its mean and standard deviation under $H_0$.

c. Find $P(\bar X\le5.46\mid\mu=6)$.

d. State the conclusion.
records.clean_answer:
a. By the central limit theorem, the sampling distribution is approximately normal.

b. Under $H_0$, $E(\bar X)=6$ and $\operatorname{SD}(\bar X)=2.47/\sqrt{100}=0.247$.

c. $z=(5.46-6)/0.247\approx-2.186$, so $P(\bar X\le5.46)\approx0.0144$.

d. This small p-value is evidence against $\mu=6$ in favor of $\mu<6$; conclude that the new system likely reduced the population mean below six minutes.

records.clean_question: In a random sample of 1,031 adults, $\hat p=0.42$ had vacationed for at least six days. To assess $H_0:p=0.40$ versus $H_a:p>0.40$, use a normal approximation to find $P(\hat p\ge0.42)$.
records.clean_answer: Under $p=0.40$, $\operatorname{SD}(\hat p)=\sqrt{0.4(0.6)/1031}\approx0.01525$. Thus $z=(0.42-0.40)/0.01525\approx1.31$, and $P(\hat p\ge0.42)\approx0.095$. The evidence is weak; at the 5% level it is not enough to conclude that more than 40% of adults meet the criterion.
